title: Constructing a Confidence Interval for a Population Mean
videoTitle: AP Statistics Topic 4.2 & 4.3 Constructing a Confidence Interval for a Population Mean
intro: Construct and interpret one-sample and paired t intervals, assess claims, and explain confidence and precision.

moments.title: Estimate a population quantity
moments.text: An interval estimates a population mean or difference of means.

moments.title: Estimate variability
moments.text: Use sample SDs when population SDs are unknown.

moments.title: Degrees of freedom
moments.text: The t reference distribution depends on degrees of freedom.

moments.title: Standard error
moments.text: Estimate the variability of the relevant sample statistic.

moments.title: Check conditions
moments.text: Justify randomization, independence, and sample-distribution requirements.

moments.title: A t critical value
moments.text: Match the confidence level and degrees of freedom to the t distribution.

moments.title: Interpret in context
moments.text: Explain confidence as a repeated-sampling capture rate.

moments.title: Assess a claim
moments.text: Compare the entire interval with the proposed population value.

cards.name: Parameter and order
cards.text: Estimate $\mu$, the population mean commute time of company employees.

cards.name: t distributions
cards.text: They are symmetric with heavier tails than the standard normal; as degrees of freedom increase, they approach standard normal.

cards.name: Conditions
cards.text: Use random data. Check sampling fractions where relevant, independence between groups, and normality or adequate sample sizes.

cards.name: Interpretation
cards.text: Confidence refers to the method's long-run capture rate. A computed interval estimates a fixed parameter.

cards.name: Width
cards.text: Higher confidence increases width; larger samples tend to reduce standard error and width, holding other features similar.

questions.obj: Construct and interpret a t interval
questions.q: The video selects 35 employees randomly, with mean commute time 28 minutes and sample SD 7.4 minutes. Construct a 90% interval for the population mean. Assume the company has at least 350 employees.

steps.t: Define the parameter and name the procedure.

work.text: Estimate $\mu$, the population mean commute time of company employees, using a one-sample t-interval.
The sample is random. The assumed population size is at least 350, satisfying the 10% condition. The sample size is at least 30.

steps.t: Calculate the point estimate and standard error.

work.text: Use the sample SD to estimate variability.

steps.t: Find the critical value and margin of error.

work.text: Use one less than the sample size for degrees of freedom.
The endpoints estimate the population parameter, not individual values.

questions.answer: We are 90% confident that the population mean commute time of company employees is between 25.885 and 30.115 minutes.

questions.obj: Construct an interval for paired differences
questions.q: Supplementary CED example: 16 randomly selected machines each complete the same task with old and new software in randomized order. Define a difference as old minus new time. The differences have mean 2.5 minutes and SD 3 minutes, with no strong skewness or outliers. Assume more than 160 eligible machines.

work.text: Estimate the population mean old-minus-new task time using a one-sample t-interval for paired differences.

steps.t: Check the differences and compute standard error.

work.text: Pairs are randomly selected, the sampling fraction is under 10%, and the differences have no strong skewness or outliers.

questions.answer: We are 95% confident that the population mean task time is 0.901 to 4.099 minutes shorter with the new software.

sections.title: Desmos walkthrough
sections.intro: The calculator starts empty. Use the menus and controls below to carry out each task yourself, then reveal the expected result.

steps.title: Enter the one-sample summary
steps.suppose: we want a 90% interval for the population mean commute time.
steps.observe: The t-test tool provides confidence intervals as well as tests. Enter the sample SD 7.4, not the standard error.

steps.title: Build the whole interval
steps.suppose: we want Desmos to calculate the endpoints.
do: On the test item, open [[Confidence Interval]].
Open the three-dot output menu at the right of the interval graphic to view numerical outputs.
Read [[Lower bound]], [[Upper bound]], [[Point estimate]], and [[Standard error]].
steps.observe: The interval estimates the population mean. Its midpoint is 28 minutes; the standard error is about 1.25083 minutes.

steps.title: Find the t critical value separately
steps.suppose: we want the critical value for 90% confidence with 34 degrees of freedom.
do: Open the distribution selector and choose [[t-distribution]].
Enter 34 for [[degrees of freedom]]. Keep shift 0 and scale 1, then press [[Create Distribution]].
Under COMPUTE choose [[Bounds]]; under REGION choose [[Inner]].
steps.observe: The bounds are symmetric. Use the positive bound as t-star. This is a separate distribution item; the interval tool already calculated the interval for you.

traps.title: Individuals versus means
traps.weak: 95% of individual values lie inside the interval.
traps.better: The interval estimates a population mean or difference of means, not the spread of individual values.

traps.title: Fixed parameter
traps.weak: There is a 95% probability that the fixed parameter is in this computed interval.
traps.better: We are 95% confident that the interval captures the parameter; the method captures it in about 95% of repeated samples.

traps.title: An interval containing zero
traps.weak: An interval containing zero proves the means are equal.
traps.better: For a difference, zero remaining plausible means the interval does not establish a nonzero population difference.

traps.title: More confidence, narrower interval
traps.better: For the same data, higher confidence requires a larger critical value and a wider interval.

notes.label: Wording check.
notes.text: The CED permits a small-sample t procedure when the relevant sample distribution is free of strong skewness and outliers; for matched pairs inspect the differences. A confidence interval does not make all parameter values equally likely.

questions.stem: An interval for a population mean is (18, 24) minutes. What is its margin of error?
For the same sample, changing confidence from 90% to 99% will:
why: A higher critical value increases the margin of error.
Greater confidence requires a wider interval.
The observed sample mean does not change.

questions.stem: A confidence interval for mean A minus mean B is (−1.2, 4.8). Which conclusion is justified?
opts: The interval does not establish a nonzero population difference
why: Both positive and negative differences remain plausible.
Containing zero does not prove equality.
Zero is included, so a nonzero difference is not established by this interval.

questions.stem: For a matched-pairs interval with 16 pairs, the standard error uses:
opts: 32 as n and both original SDs
The SD of the 16 differences divided by 4
A standard normal critical value automatically
why: There are 16 independent differences, not 32 independent measurements.
Use the sample of differences: s_d/√16.
The SD of differences depends on pairing, not subtraction of SDs.
With an unknown population SD, a t method is appropriate.

sections.title: Write a complete response
sections.prompt: A random sample of 36 maintenance jobs from a population of 2,000 has mean completion time 54 minutes and sample SD 9 minutes.
parts: (a) Define the parameter and check conditions for a 95% interval.
(c) Interpret the interval and explain what 95% confidence means.
sample: (a) The parameter is the population mean completion time for these maintenance jobs. Use a one-sample t-interval. The sample is random, 36≤0.10(2000), and n≥30.
(b) SE=9/√36=1.5 minutes, df=35, and the 95% interval is (50.955, 57.045) minutes.

(c) We are 95% confident that the population mean completion time is between 50.955 and 57.045 minutes. In repeated random samples of 36, about 95% of intervals built this way capture the fixed population mean.
checklist: Defines the population mean in context.
Checks randomness, sampling fraction, and sample size.
Interprets both the interval and the long-run confidence level.
